title: Orders close: many rooms
hook: five families of prayer, one house: looking back on the great orders

segments.voice: Yesterday, simple attention, Carmel's plainest prayer. Your line was loving attention. Which chore became a place to look at God? Day one thousand two hundred ninety-one.

A bell in a monastery calling monks from the garden to the chapel. A barefoot friar, patient and glad in the cold. A preacher with a book under his arm. A soldier-turned-pilgrim asking what stirs in his heart. A hermit's cell on a mountain, and a silence you could lean against. That's the road this block has walked: the great orders of the Catholic Church, one family after another. Today we stand at the end of the corridor and look back at all the doors. Today, the orders close.
screen: `A BELL, A FRIAR, A BOOK.` → `A HEART, A SILENCE.` → `ALL THE DOORS AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: First, Benedict's balance. Ora et labora, pray and work: a day where the bell, the psalm, the garden and the meal each get their place, and none swallows the rest. Second, Francis's joy. Not a cheerful mood, but perfect joy, the kind that stays patient even when you're turned away in the cold. Third, Dominic's truth. Veritas, the order's motto: pray, study, and then share what you've found, because truth is meant to be handed on. Fourth, Ignatius's discernment, reading the movements of the heart to find God in all things. And fifth, Carmel's silence: the cell, the desert, the friend, the night, and simple loving attention. Five families, five ways in. Now the image that holds them. Jesus tells his friends at the Last Supper, in the Douay-Rheims: "In my Father's house there are many mansions." Many rooms, one house. The Church doesn't ask anyone to live in all five rooms at once, and it doesn't rank them. Saint Paul says it to the Corinthians: "Now there are diversities of graces, but the same Spirit." A Benedictine and a Jesuit pray very differently, and both are at home. That's the surprise of this block: the orders aren't rival teams. They are rooms in one house, and a person can be drawn to one room for a season of life, then find another door opening years later. Not everyone will take vows. But anyone can borrow a room: an hour of balance, a moment of joy, one shared truth, a nightly examen, a few minutes of silence.
screen: `BALANCE AND JOY.` · `TRUTH AND DISCERNMENT.` · `CARMEL'S SILENCE.` · then, large: `IN MY FATHER'S HOUSE, MANY MANSIONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one room to live in this month. Settle, and breathe. Walk slowly past each door in your mind. Benedict's: a day balanced between work and prayer. Francis's: joy and simplicity. Dominic's: study and sharing one true thing. Ignatius's: the examen each night. Carmel's: a few minutes of silent, loving attention. Don't pick the one that sounds most impressive. Notice which door your heart leans toward, and stop there. If you pray, you can ask God to show you the room for this season. If you don't, simply trust the lean. The bell holds the time.
Orders close. The end of the great orders: Benedict's balance, Francis's joy, Dominic's truth, Ignatius's discernment, Carmel's silence, rooms in one house. Today's word.

Your line: many rooms, one house. Today, write down the room you chose, and one small way you'll live in it this month. Tomorrow a new block begins: the Church's teaching on justice. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: Catholics who aren't in religious life often draw on one order's spirituality: some become oblates of a Benedictine monastery, secular Franciscans, lay Dominicans or Secular Carmelites, or keep an Ignatian examen, while staying in their parish.

what a scholar hears: monē in John 14:2, a dwelling place, and Paul's diversities of graces, one Spirit, as the frame for the Church's many charisms.
